# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are team communication platforms that enable real-time messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and customization. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and infrastructure.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to host their own data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Element can be more scalable with proper self-hosting.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption, while Slack does not have this feature by default.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Wide range of integrations
* Good mobile apps
* Limited control over data and infrastructure
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* End-to-end encryption
* High degree of customization
* Good for teams with high security requirements
* Limited user base and community compared to Slack

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying per user. It's ideal for large teams and enterprises that need a scalable solution with a wide range of integrations. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that prioritize data ownership and customization. It's ideal for teams with high security requirements, such as those in the finance or healthcare industries.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure your Element instance to match your Slack setup.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires a high degree of technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's scalability can be limited by the resources available on the self-hosted server. However, for teams that prioritize data ownership and customization, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element if you have a small to medium-sized team with high security requirements.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need a wide range of integrations
* Teams with high security requirements (e.g. finance, healthcare)
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and customization
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user fees
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle self-hosting and maintenance

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted. You only need to pay for the server costs.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a wide range of integrations available, although not as many as Slack.
### Is Element more secure than Slack?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption, which makes it more secure than Slack.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, compared to Slack's straightforward signup process.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility in terms of customization and control.
* Integration Difference: Mattermost has a more extensive range of customization options and integrations with other tools, particularly for development teams, through its open-source nature.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Strong support and community
* User-friendly interface
* Limitation: Less control over data and higher costs for large teams
### Mattermost
* Free, self-hosted option
* High level of customization and control
* Open-source and extensible
* Strong security features
* Limitation: Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance, and may have a steeper learning curve

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, particularly small to medium-sized teams or those without extensive technical expertise. It's ideal for teams that need a straightforward, user-friendly communication platform without the need for deep customization or control over their data.
Mattermost is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their data, customization options, and security features. It's particularly suitable for development teams or those with the technical expertise to set up and maintain a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack Export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON files exported from Slack.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your team's needs, including setting up channels, users, and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure all features and data are working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is production-ready for most users, offering a stable and feature-rich platform for team communication. However, it's essential to consider the technical requirements and potential learning curve associated with setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution.
One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile apps may not offer the same level of polish or features as Slack's, which could impact user adoption.
For teams prioritizing data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness, switching to Mattermost is a clear recommendation, especially for larger teams or those with technical expertise. However, smaller teams or those without extensive technical resources may find Slack's ease of use and wide range of integrations more appealing.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) seeking to reduce costs and gain more control over their data
* Development teams requiring a high level of customization and integration with other tools
* Organizations prioritizing data security and compliance, particularly those in regulated industries
* Teams with existing self-hosted infrastructure, looking to leverage their existing resources
* Educational institutions or non-profits seeking a free, self-hosted communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, allowing teams to host their own servers and avoid per-user costs.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, particularly for self-hosting, but offers a more customizable and controllable platform.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with other tools?
Yes, Mattermost has a wide range of integrations with other tools, particularly through its open-source nature and extensible architecture.
### Does Mattermost offer mobile apps?
Yes, Mattermost offers mobile apps for both iOS and Android, although they may not offer the same level of polish or features as Slack's.
### Can I export my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack Export tool and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations seeking a secure, self-hosted alternative to traditional proprietary platforms. The core use case for both tools is real-time communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and hosting.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's terms of service grant the company access to user data.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is designed to be highly scalable, with support for large communities and organizations, while Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Discord
* Easy to use and set up
* Large user base and community
* Supports screen sharing and video conferencing
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data and hosting
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Supports bridge to other platforms (e.g., Matrix, Slack)
* Steeper learning curve and technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams, gaming communities, or individuals who prioritize ease of use and a large user base. It is ideal for those who do not require advanced security features or control over their data. On the other hand, Element is designed for organizations and communities that value security, scalability, and customizability. It is perfect for large teams, enterprises, or individuals who require advanced features and control over their data.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Import your Discord data into Element using the Element import tool or a third-party script.
4. Configure bridges to other platforms (if necessary) and test your Element setup.
5. Update your community or team on the migration and provide support during the transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise and has a steeper learning curve. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's federation protocol can be complex to set up and manage. However, for organizations and communities that value security and control over their data, Element is a clear choice. We recommend switching to Element if you prioritize advanced security features, self-hosting, and customizability.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized teams (less than 50 users) that require advanced security features and control over their data
* Gaming communities that do not need screen sharing or video conferencing
* Enterprises with large teams (over 200 users) that require customizability and scalability
* Organizations that prioritize self-hosting and data ownership
* Individuals who do not need mobile apps or a large user base

## FAQ

No, Element is a separate platform with its own protocol, but it supports bridges to other platforms.

Yes, you can export your Discord data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
### Is Element suitable for small teams?
Yes, Element is suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and manage.

# Notion vs AppFlowy (2026)

* Data ownership: AppFlowy allows users to self-host their data, giving them full ownership and control, whereas Notion stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Notion has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while AppFlowy requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: AppFlowy is designed to be highly scalable, especially when self-hosted, whereas Notion's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.

|--------|----------|---------|

| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1600-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

* Easy to use and set up
* Extensive library of third-party integrations
* Robust customer support

### AppFlowy
* Free and open-source

AppFlowy, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of customization, scalability, and data control. * Large teams (50+ users) seeking to reduce costs
* Technical teams that require self-hosting and full data control
* Organizations with high scalability requirements
* Teams that do not require a wide range of third-party integrations

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Obsidian is a free, self-hosted alternative to Notion. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage and collaborate on software projects. This comparison is useful for individuals and teams who are considering switching from one platform to the other, particularly those who value data ownership and customizability. The core use case for both platforms is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and workflows.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free public repositories, but charges for private repositories, while GitLab offers free self-hosted repositories with optional paid support.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more streamlined setup process, while GitLab requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosted instances.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more customization and control over scalability.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers built-in CI/CD pipelines, while GitHub requires third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free public repositories
* Limited customization options for free plan
**GitLab:**
* Offers self-hosted option for full data control
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Built-in CI/CD pipelines
* Free self-hosted option with optional paid support
* Steeper learning curve due to complexity

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who prioritize ease of use and don't require a high degree of customization. It's also a good option for open-source projects that require a large community and ecosystem. On the other hand, GitLab is a good choice for larger teams or enterprises that require more control over their data and workflows. It's also a good option for teams that need a high degree of customization and extensibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which generates a zip file containing your repository data.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the repository settings.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to import your GitHub repository data from the zip file.
4. Update any dependencies or integrations to point to your new GitLab repository.
5. Test your repository to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data and workflows. However, one technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted option requires significant technical expertise to set up and configure. For teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require a high degree of customization, GitHub may still be a better option. However, for teams that require more control over their data and workflows, GitLab is a clear winner.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need GitHub's large community and ecosystem
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who require more customization options than GitHub's free plan offers
* Large teams (more than 50 users) who require self-hosted repositories for data control
* Enterprises that require a high degree of customization and extensibility
* Teams that need built-in CI/CD pipelines and don't want to rely on third-party integrations

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with optional paid support.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, GitLab offers an import tool that allows you to migrate your GitHub repository data.
### Is GitLab more secure than GitHub?
Both platforms have robust security features, but GitLab's self-hosted option gives users more control over their data and security.
### Can I use GitLab for open-source projects?
Yes, GitLab is a good option for open-source projects that require a high degree of customization and control.
### Does GitLab offer a free trial?
No, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with optional paid support, but does not offer a free trial for its paid support plans.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
